title: Prefix-to-place geocoder
summary: Map a number to its city/region, and a place back to a prefix
description:
CURRENT STATE: nothing built. The `phonenumber` crate provides parse/validate/format but has NO geocoder — verified against its docs. We implement this ourselves over libphonenumber's geocoding data files, which F003 packages.

WHAT THE DATA LOOKS LIKE: plain prefix-to-place text, e.g. for Italy — 39010|Genova, 39011|Torino, 390121|Pinerolo. 151 countries, 34 languages, 11 MB raw.

TWO DIRECTIONS, BOTH NEEDED:
- geocode(E164, language) -> Country / Region / City, for showing where a number is from.
- place -> prefix, because a location rule IS a prefix rule (recorded decision). "Block Genova" resolves to prefix 39010 and then goes through normal expansion.

IMPLEMENTATION: longest-prefix match over a trie. Must be fast and low-memory — it runs inside the iOS extension.

LANGUAGE FALLBACK (R7): user's language, then English, then the bare prefix with no place name. Never a blank and never an untranslated key. Coverage is uneven — English is most complete at 151 countries; China has 130,165 entries, Turkmenistan has 5.

THE CAVEAT THAT MUST REACH THE UI: mobile numbers have NO geocoding data anywhere, because mobile numbering is not geographic. Verified: Italy has 0 entries for 393xx and 121 for 390xx. So location rules match landlines only. The geocoder must return a distinct "not geographic" answer rather than an empty one, so the UI can say why instead of showing nothing.

SECOND CAVEAT: number portability erodes even landline accuracy. Worth surfacing as approximate rather than authoritative.

COUNTERINTUITIVE PROPERTY WORTH KNOWING: a longer prefix leaves fewer digits to expand, so smaller towns fit more easily than big cities. Pinerolo (390121) is cheaper to block than Genova (39010).

tasks.title: Geocode a number to a place, with language fallback
tasks.description:
DEPENDS ON P006(F003)/T015, which packs the place data. core/src/dataset.rs already provides Dataset::lookup(digits) doing longest-prefix match, so the lookup itself exists; this is the layer above it.

CURRENT STATE. Nothing in the core geocodes. The packed datasets build to datasets/build/places.<lang>.cfds and nothing loads them.

GOAL. geocode(number, languages, datasets) -> Located, in core/src/geocode.rs (new). Serves R7's place-name half and the display side of R2.

THE ANSWER IS NOT A STRING. There are at least three outcomes and they are different things to say:
- a place name, plus which language it came from, because that is not always the one asked for;
- NOT GEOGRAPHIC — the number is a mobile, and mobile numbering is not tied to a place anywhere in the world. VERIFIED 2026-09-10: Italy has 0 geocoding entries for 393 (mobile) and 121 for 390 (landline). Returning "nothing found" here would be a lie; the UI must be able to say why;
- no data — the country or prefix simply is not covered.
Collapsing these into Option<String> loses exactly the honesty R2 and R8 ask for.

LANGUAGE FALLBACK (R7), in order: the user's language, then English, then the bare prefix with no name. Never a blank, never an untranslated key. This is the NORMAL path, not an edge case — measured coverage: English 151 countries; Italian 2; German 5; Chinese 2. An Italian user gets Italian names for Italy and Switzerland and English everywhere else.

ACCURACY IS APPROXIMATE, and the type should not pretend otherwise. Number portability means a landline can keep its number after moving. The data is a good guide, not a fact about where a caller is.

WHAT TO BUILD:
1. A Located result covering the cases above, carrying the language actually used.
2. A holder for several loaded datasets, ordered by preference, that tries each in turn.
3. Loading datasets from bytes. The core must not read files — the shells own IO — so take bytes or an already-parsed Dataset.
4. Deciding "not geographic" from the number's type via the phonenumber metadata, not by guessing from an empty lookup: a missing entry and a mobile are different answers.

CONSTRAINTS.
- Guidelines §1: no country, prefix or place name in code.
- Guidelines §5 / R7: no user-facing English in the core. Return facts and let the shell word them.
- Runs app-side, not in the iOS extension — see the note in core/src/dataset.rs.

EDGE CASES to test: a landline in a covered country; a mobile in the same country; a country with no data in any loaded language; a language that covers the country and one that does not, proving fallback; an empty dataset list; a number shorter than any prefix; the same number in two languages giving two names.

DONE WHEN. Every case above is distinguishable in the result, fallback is proven by test rather than asserted, and cargo test / fmt / clippy -D warnings / both lints pass. Fixtures in core/tests/.

---
**Completion summary:**
SHIPPED. Commit 67bd36a.

core/src/geocode.rs (new), core/tests/geocode.rs (13 tests), core/tests/real_check.rs (1 ignored test against the real packed data). expand.rs::descriptors_of made pub(crate) so the number-type taxonomy is listed once.

API. geocode(number, &Places, &Database) -> Located, and is_geographic(number, &Database) -> bool. Places holds parsed datasets in preference order; the core never opens a file, because an iOS extension and an Android app disagree about where bytes come from.

A CRATE BUG, FOUND AND WORKED AROUND — the substance of this task. PhoneNumber::number_type builds the national number with `value().to_string()`, which drops leading zeros. Italy's leading zero is part of the number, so number_type returns Unknown for EVERY Italian landline. The crate's own is_valid_with uses `Display`, which keeps the zeros, so the two disagree: +390111234567 is valid and typeless at the same time. Probed directly:
  +390111234567  valid=true  type=Unknown
  +442012345678  valid=true  type=FixedLine
  +393331234567  valid=true  type=Mobile
Geography is therefore derived here from the Display form and the descriptors, not from number_type. Without this every Italian landline would have reported NotGeographic and nothing would have failed.

THE SAME BUG BIT THE DATASET KEY. digits_of first used `national().value()`, producing 39111234567 where the data is keyed 39011234567, so every Italian lookup missed. Both now go through Display. This is the third time the trunk-zero has caused a silent wrong answer in this project — the first was in normalize (T006). Worth remembering that in this crate `value()` is almost always the wrong one to reach for.

DECISION — three outcomes, not Option<String>. Place{name, language}, NotGeographic, NoData, plus NotANumber. A mobile and an uncovered country both find nothing in the place data, and they are completely different things to tell someone: one is a gap that better packaging would close, the other is a question that does not apply anywhere in the world. Verified against the real data: Italy has 0 geocoding entries for 393 and 121 for 390.

DECISION — is_geographic is public separately. A location rule cannot match a mobile, and the UI must say so while the rule is being written rather than when a call slips through. It needs no place data, only the metadata.

DECISION — FixedLineOrMobile counts as geographic. In territories that cannot tell the two apart the fixed-line pattern matches, and refusing to look would throw away a usable answer for every number in those countries. Unknown does not short-circuit either: claiming a number is nowhere on the strength of metadata that does not recognise it would overstate what is known, so the lookup proceeds and the data answers.

The result carries which language answered. English covers 151 countries and Italian covers 2, so falling back is the normal path and the UI should not have to guess which language it is showing.

VERIFIED. cargo test --all: 133 pass, 2 ignored, 0 fail. fmt, clippy --all-targets -D warnings, §1 lint and the vendored-data check all clean. UniFFI bindings still generate. Against the REAL packed datasets, not only fixtures: +390111234567 to Torino (it), +390101234567 to Genova (it), +390212345678 to Milano (it), +442012345678 to London (en) by fallback, +393331234567 to NotGeographic. That test is ignored by default because it needs build-datasets to have run first.

NOT DONE HERE. The reverse direction — a place to its prefixes — is P004(F002)/T017, which also has to fix the one-prefix assumption in PrefixSource: "Turin" is 3 prefixes in the Italian data and "Guangzhou, Guangdong" is 1,565, so a location rule today would silently block a fraction of a city. Nothing loads datasets from disk in the core, by design. Nothing is exported over UniFFI; that is P005.

UNVERIFIED. Never run on a device or through Swift or Kotlin. Accuracy is approximate by nature — numbers are portable, so the data says where a number was issued, not where the caller is. That caveat is documented in the module but has no expression in the type, and the UI will need to carry it.

tasks.title: Resolve a place to its prefixes, fixing the one-prefix assumption
tasks.description:
DEPENDS ON P004(F002)/T016 for the dataset holder.

A BUG IN THE RULE MODEL, found while reading the real data on 2026-09-10. P002(F002)/T004 defined:

    pub trait PrefixSource {
        fn prefix_for(&self, location: &LocationRef) -> Option<Digits>;
    }

and Authored::Location resolves through it to exactly one Matcher::StartsWith. THE DATA DOES NOT WORK THAT WAY. A city routinely has several area codes:
- "Turin" appears 3 times in the Italian data (39011, 390122, 390125).
- "Guangzhou, Guangdong" appears 1,565 times in the Chinese data.

So "block Turin" cannot be represented today. The current model would silently pick one prefix and block a third of the city, which is precisely the silent narrowing R2 forbids. Nothing fails: the rule looks fine, and calls from the other two area codes get through.

GOAL. Make a location resolve to the SET of prefixes that name it, and carry that through the model, the evaluator and expansion without any of them special-casing location.

WHAT TO BUILD:
1. Replace prefix_for with something returning all matching prefixes. Keep it a trait so the geocoder is injected rather than reached for.
2. Decide how a multi-prefix location is represented. Two candidates, and this is the real design decision of the task:
   - resolve one authored rule into several rules, one per prefix — simple, but rule ids stop being one-to-one with what the user wrote, and the UI has to re-group them to show one rule;
   - give Matcher a variant matching any of a set of prefixes — one rule stays one rule, but specificity, overlap and expansion all need to handle it.
   Whichever is chosen, write down why in the completion, because both have a cost that shows up later.
3. Specificity for a multi-prefix match. Prefixes for one city are usually different lengths (39011 is 5, 390122 is 6). The safe reading is the SHORTEST, since that is the broadest thing the rule matches — but say so explicitly rather than leaving it to fall out.
4. Expansion must cover every prefix, and the result must still be ascending and free of duplicates. Two area codes of a city can overlap in the block list.
5. Matching a place name is not exact-string business: names carry a region suffix ("Guangzhou, Guangdong"), and the UI will offer a picked place rather than typed text. Decide what a LocationRef actually holds and keep it opaque to the core.

ALSO REQUIRED BY R2. Location rules match landlines only, because mobile numbering is not geographic anywhere. Verified: Italy has 0 geocoding entries for 393 and 121 for 390. A location rule therefore cannot block a mobile, and explain() should say so on every surface.

CONSTRAINTS.
- Guidelines §1: no country, prefix or place name in code.
- Guidelines §3: this is filtering logic, so it lives in the core.
- The evaluator's matching path must stay allocation-free.

EDGE CASES to test: a place with one prefix; a place with three; a place with over a thousand; a place that resolves to nothing, which is legal because metadata changes; two places whose prefixes overlap; a location rule against a country with no geocoding data at all; the same place name in two languages.

DONE WHEN. A location rule with several prefixes blocks all of them, is one rule to the user, expansion stays ascending and duplicate-free, explain() reports the landline-only limit, every P002 and P003 test still passes, and cargo test / fmt / clippy -D warnings / both lints pass.

checklist.title: PrefixSource replaced with something returning every matching prefix
Multi-prefix representation chosen, with the reason recorded
Specificity for a multi-prefix location defined deliberately, not incidentally
Expansion covers every prefix, still ascending and duplicate-free
LocationRef contents decided and kept opaque to the core
explain() reports that location rules cannot match mobiles
Edge cases: one, three, 1000+, none, overlapping, uncovered country, two languages
All P002 and P003 tests still pass
cargo test, fmt, clippy -D warnings, both lints
